<Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott, Rep. Suzanne Bonamici, Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, Rep. Jahana Hayes, Rep. Adelita S. Grijalva>: In determining grants under national activities, current law permits the Secretary to give priority to charter management organizations that: will serve racially and socioeconomically diverse student populations; have demonstrated success with schools needing comprehensive support and improvement; will use funds to expand or replicate high-quality charter high schools; or plan to focus on dropout recovery.\53\ All four of these priorities focus on students. In contrast, H.R. 7082 would add a priority for applications by charter management organizations that plan to enter a state in which they do not currently operate a charter school or a state ``with limited charter school options.''\54\ This priority demonstrates greater interest in expanding the management organization rather than in serving the students who need it most. Moreover, it is unclear what constitutes a state ``with limited charter school options''' or how that would be determined. Considering that charter school laws are determined by each state, this seems an odd interference by the federal government.
\53\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221d(b)(5).
\54\H.R. 7082 Sec. 4, 119th Cong. (2026).
In addition, the fact that the bill slashes funding for high-quality charter schools in order to increase funding for charter management organizations does not consider that demand for CSP funding has declined in recent years. In 2024, the Biden Administration indicated that the demand for CSP funding to open and expand charter schools declined from 2019 to 2023, and that awards were reduced due to the inability to meet grantees' original targets.\55\ In 2023 2024, there were 8,010 charter schools.\56\ In 2024 2025, there were only 38 more (8,048).\57\ Still, President Trump's Fiscal Year (FY) 2026 budget proposal included a $60 million (14%) increase to CSP for a total of $500 million,\58\ and on May 16, 2025, Education Secretary McMahon announced that the Department would give CSP an additional $60 million in funding for FY 2025, unilaterally effectuating the President's request for that fiscal year.\59\ President Trump's FY 2027 budget again requests Congress to increase CSP funding to $500 million.\60\ Despite the dwindling demand for new charter schools, the need for funding across so many areas of education, and inflation that continues to outpace appropriations, this bill would take funding away from students and classrooms and instead give it to charter management organizations.
\55\U.S. Dep't of Educ., Fiscal Year 2025 Justifications of Appropriation Estimates--Innovation and Improvement at 41-42 (2024), FY 2025 Congressional Justification Innovation and Improvement.
\56\U.S. Dep't of Educ., Nat'l Ctr. for Educ. Stats., Common Core of Data, Table 3. Number of operating public elementary and secondary schools, by school type, charter, and state or jurisdiction: School year 2023-24, https://nces.ed.gov/ccd/tables/202324_summary_3.asp (last visited Mar. 11, 2026).
\57\U.S. Dep't of Educ., Nat'l Ctr. for Educ. Stats., Common Core of Data, Table 3. Number of operating public elementary and secondary schools, by school type, charter, and state or jurisdiction: School year 2024-25, https://nces.ed.gov/ccd/tables/202425_summary_3.asp (last visited Mar. 11, 2026).
\58\The White House, President Trump's Fiscal Year 2026 Discretionary Funding Request at 2, https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/President-Trumps-Fiscal-Year-2026- Discretionary-Funding-Request-Overview.pdf (last visited Mar. 11, 2026).
\59\Press Release, U.S. Dep't of Educ., Secretary McMahon Announces Immediate Increased Funding, New Grant Program for Charter Schools (May 16, 2025), https://www.ed.gov/about/news/press-release/secretary-mcmahon-announces-immediate-increased-funding-new-grant-program-charter-schools.
\60\U.S. Dep't of Educ. Fiscal Year 2027 Budget Summary at 6, https://www.ed.gov/media/ document/fy-2027-budget-summary-113552.pdf (last visited Apr. 13, 2026).
H.R. 7082 Would Negatively Alter Definitions and Applicability
H.R. 7082 Would Sow Confusion Regarding the Definition of
Charter School
Current law defines a charter school as ``a public school that provides a program of elementary or secondary education, or both.''\61\ H.R. 7082 would change the definition of a charter school to ``a public school that provides a program of elementary or secondary education (which may include other educational programs, pursuant to State law), or both.''\62\ The bill's language is confusing and its intent is unclear. Further, the new language could create inconsistency across states. For example, it is unclear if the new language is age related, so intended to permit, for example, early childhood education as part of a charter school (which is already permitted) or adult education or something else. Alternatively, it is unclear if the language is intended to be program specific, so intended to permit, for example, a school focused solely on a specific disability. This lack of a clear definition of what constitutes a charter school--the most fundamental definition necessary for this entire program-- exemplifies the lack of clarity and transparency found throughout the bill.
\61\20 U.S.C. Sec. 7221i(2)(D).
\62\H.R. 7082 Sec. 7, 119th Cong. (2026) (emphasis added).
H.R. 7082 Would Allow Grantees to Decide When to Apply to
the Law
Rather than applying the changes to the law on or after the date of enactment should the legislation become law, H.R. 7082 would permit current grantees and subgrantees to decide whether they want the changes to apply to them.\63\ This would make applicability inconsistent and enable grantees and subgrantees to unilaterally self-elect to change the terms of their grant or subgrant contracts. In other words, this provision would leave it up to the states to decide whether to enact or enforce federal law and would make it impossible for the federal government to conduct its own responsibilities to implement the law and conduct oversight over a federal program and how federal taxpayer dollars are spent.
\63\H.R. 7082 Sec. 8, 119th Cong. (2026).
DEMOCRATIC AMENDMENTS OFFERED DURING THE MARKUP OF H.R. 7082
Committee Democrats proffered three amendments to improve the bill. These amendments would have prohibited funding from being used for virtual charters schools, required charter funding applicants to assess segregation in the community and propose how to address it, and required a study to identify disparities and address discrimination of historically underrepresented students in and by charter schools. Committee Republicans rejected all three Democratic amendments that were considered.

CONCLUSION
H.R. 7082 would provide greater flexibility for charter schools but only at the expense of taking money from students and classrooms, eliminating guardrails and oversight, and increasing the risk of greater waste, fraud, and abuse of taxpayer dollars. For the reasons stated above, all Committee Democrats present opposed H.R. 7082 when the Committee on Education and Workforce considered it on January 21, 2026. We urge the House of Representatives to do the same.
Robert C. ``Bobby'' Scott,
Ranking Member.
Suzanne Bonamici,
